Source: Urban Affairs Review

Why included: Canadian-affiliated author or institution; Canada-related term in abstract: canada, quebec

Abstract: This article examines citizens’ satisfaction with their municipal democracy according to whether mayoral elections were competitive or non-competitive. After defining different types of satisfaction and based on a survey of 4,026 respondents in the province of Quebec (Canada), we show that citizens living in municipalities where elections were non-competitive are more satisfied with the mayor than citizens living in municipalities where elections were competitive. These results suggest that—in the eyes of some voters—the mere fact that a citizen is available to hold office is sufficient to ensure democracy. More generally, our results underline the need for a detailed understanding of citizen satisfaction and the different ways in which it can be expressed in the various contexts and electoral mechanisms in force.
